steps.premise: Several makers may put similar bowls together on the rack.
steps.action: Leave reusable name cards and a pencil at the rack so each maker can label a board before others add their work.
steps.consequence: The maker can identify which board is theirs.
steps.quote: Keep a pencil and reusable name cards by the rack so a maker can claim a board before a dozen similar bowls land beside it.

steps.premise: Some shelves are too deep to reach from the front.
steps.action: Keep a path open to the back of those shelves.
steps.consequence: People can reach their work without leaning over freshly made rims.
steps.quote: If a shelf is too deep to reach across from one side, leave access behind it so nobody has to lean over a row of fresh rims.

steps.premise: In dim light a low dish at the back can look like an empty space.
steps.action: Direct a small lamp along the back of the shelf.
steps.consequence: Users can tell which spaces are available.
steps.quote: A small lamp aimed along the back of a dim shelf makes an empty spot easier to distinguish from a space occupied by a low dish.

steps.premise: Beginners may be unsure how far apart to put pots.
steps.action: Show a board on the teaching table with enough space between pots for a hand.
steps.consequence: Beginners can judge the spacing before loading their own boards.
steps.quote: Leave an example board on the teaching table with the pots spaced for a hand to pass between them. Beginners can see how much room to allow before they load their own.

steps.premise: A stack of unused boards can resemble work already on the rack.
steps.action: Store spare boards on their own stand near the worktables.
steps.consequence: Students can distinguish board supplies from occupied drying space.
steps.quote: Keep empty boards on a separate stand near the worktables so students don't mistake a supply pile for occupied drying space.

steps.premise: A piece may need attention while its maker is away.
steps.action: Let members name someone to check their pieces during an absence.
steps.consequence: Staff know whom to ask about the work.
steps.quote: Let members nominate someone to check their work during an absence, giving staff a known person to ask if a piece needs attention.

steps.premise: Whether an order can be filled depends on the date and number of chairs.
steps.action: List the available chair count for each date on the shared booking calendar.
steps.consequence: Organizers can tell whether enough chairs are available for their event.
steps.quote: Put the number of available chairs against each date on a shared booking calendar so organizers can see whether a request will fit.

steps.premise: A delayed driver may need to reach the person who can unlock the venue.
steps.action: Ask each organizer to identify a contact who can be reached during the event.
steps.consequence: The driver can call the keyholder if running late.
steps.quote: Have each organizer name someone reachable during the event. A driver running late can call the person with the keys.

steps.premise: A damaged chair might go out with the next order.
steps.action: Give chairs with a loose hinge or missing foot a visible repair tag and put them in a separate spot.
steps.consequence: The next delivery excludes chairs that need repair.
steps.quote: Give a chair with a loose hinge or missing foot a conspicuous repair tag and a separate storage spot, keeping it out of the next delivery.

steps.premise: Chairs can come back wet.
steps.action: Provide a sheltered area for opening the returned chairs and drying them.
steps.consequence: They are dry when they go back into storage.
steps.quote: Provide a sheltered place to unfold wet returns and let them dry before they go back into storage.

steps.premise: Organizers may need to mark reserved seats on chairs they have borrowed.
steps.action: Lend the event team removable signs that clip onto rows.
steps.consequence: They can reserve seats without leaving adhesive behind.
steps.quote: Give the event team removable row signs that clip on. They can reserve seats without leaving tape or adhesive on borrowed chairs.

steps.premise: The organizer may have to leave before the chairs are due back.
steps.action: Let the borrower designate someone else to return them.
steps.consequence: The chairs can still be returned on time.
steps.quote: Let a borrower nominate another person to make the return so the chairs can get back on time even when the event organizer has to leave early.

steps.premise: An audible event can explain a reaction that is hard to understand from the dialogue alone.
steps.action: Briefly describe the sound in the captions when it helps explain the speakers’ response.
steps.consequence: Visitors following the captions can understand the reaction.
steps.quote: Include a brief description of a meaningful sound, such as the train whistle both speakers stop to hear, when it helps explain their reaction.

steps.premise: Visitors need to take in captions at a glance.
steps.action: Break lines at natural points and keep the parts of a person’s name on the same line.
steps.consequence: The reader can grasp the phrasing and the name quickly.
steps.quote: Break lines at natural points in a sentence and keep a person's first and last name together to make the text easier to take in at a glance.

steps.premise: The flow of a reply can be hard to follow from the captions alone.
steps.action: Have a reviewer follow an entire interview on mute and mark any reply that seems unexplained.
steps.consequence: The reviewer identifies gaps in what the captions communicate.
steps.quote: Ask a reviewer to follow a complete interview with the sound muted and flag places where a reply seems to come out of nowhere.

steps.premise: Staff need to know where in a recording a visitor noticed an error.
steps.action: Provide a correction slip that asks for the interview title and playback time.
steps.consequence: Staff can locate the reported error.
steps.quote: Give visitors a correction slip with space for the interview title and playback time so staff can find a reported error.

steps.premise: When a narrator reads a letter or diary aloud, the words belong to the quoted writer.
steps.action: Identify the excerpt in the captions as the reading begins.
steps.consequence: Visitors can tell whose words they are following.
steps.quote: Introduce a recorded letter or diary excerpt in the captions when a narrator starts reading aloud, so visitors know whose words are being quoted.

steps.premise: People may arrive partway through a looped exhibit.
steps.action: Keep the interview title visible beside the captions.
steps.consequence: A visitor who missed the beginning can identify the story.
steps.quote: For an exhibit that plays on a loop, display the interview title alongside the captions so someone arriving midway can place the story.

steps.premise: A newcomer may arrive without seeing anyone they know.
steps.action: Station a host at the entrance to greet arrivals and offer to walk them to the lesson.
steps.consequence: A first-time visitor can join the lesson without searching for a familiar face.
steps.quote: Have a host meet people at the door and offer to walk them over to the lesson, sparing a first-time visitor the search for a familiar face.

steps.premise: Guests may be unsure how to invite someone or decline comfortably.
steps.action: Demonstrate a friendly invitation and a friendly decline during the welcome.
steps.consequence: Guests hear how the exchange can end comfortably whichever answer is given.
steps.quote: Model both a friendly invitation and a friendly decline during the welcome. Guests get to hear how either answer can end comfortably.

steps.premise: Beginners need time to decide whether to join a particular dance.
steps.action: Name the dance before the music starts.
steps.consequence: They can decide whether to get up before it begins.
steps.quote: Announce the type of dance before the music starts so a beginner has time to decide whether to get up for it.

steps.premise: Some dancers find spinning uncomfortable.
steps.action: Teach an easier version of the turn with both feet close to the floor.
steps.consequence: They can still perform the figure.
steps.quote: Show an easy version of a turn that keeps both feet close to the floor, giving anyone who finds spinning uncomfortable a way through the figure.

steps.premise: Room noise can make spoken demonstrations hard to follow.
steps.action: Light the teacher’s face and feet well during demonstrations.
steps.consequence: Learners can follow the visual cues.
steps.quote: Keep the teacher's face and feet well lit during demonstrations so people can use visual cues when the room is noisy.

steps.premise: People who sit out several songs may miss chances to get to know others.
steps.action: Turn down the music during a break and invite a short conversation.
steps.consequence: People can meet the group even if they have been sitting out.
steps.quote: Invite people to chat briefly over a break with the music turned down. Someone who sat out a few songs can still get to know the group.

steps.premise: Someone without an oven may have a local loaf worth sharing.
steps.action: Welcome bread bought at a favorite neighborhood bakery.
steps.consequence: People without ovens can contribute a loaf and introduce it to the group.
steps.quote: Welcome a loaf from a favorite neighborhood bakery. Someone without an oven can make an introduction every bit as interesting as a home baker's.

steps.premise: A crust may hide what is in or on a loaf.
steps.action: Put blank ingredient cards by the bread with space to record fillings and toppings.
steps.consequence: Guests can identify ingredients they cannot see from the outside.
steps.quote: Put blank ingredient cards beside the bread and leave room for fillings and toppings, which can be hard to identify from the crust.

steps.premise: Standing for long can tire some participants.
steps.action: Provide a stool at the exchange table.
steps.consequence: They can stay longer and talk with bakers.
steps.quote: A stool at the exchange table gives anyone who tires of standing a chance to linger and talk to the bakers.

steps.premise: Starting a conversation with strangers can feel awkward.
steps.action: Invite contributors to leave a short account of their loaf’s history beside it.
steps.consequence: Guests have something specific to ask about when starting a conversation.
steps.quote: Invite people to put a few words about a loaf's history beside it. Asking about a grandmother's skillet bread is an easier opening than introducing yourself to a room.

steps.premise: A failed batch may leave someone with nothing to bring.
steps.action: Reserve a basket of spare contributions for guests who arrive empty-handed.
steps.consequence: They can still come and take part in the swap.
steps.quote: Set a basket of spare contributions aside for people who turn up empty-handed. A batch that didn't rise shouldn't have to keep a neighbor away.

steps.premise: Newcomers may feel awkward guessing a fair portion.
steps.action: Place an actual example of the suggested portion near the entrance.
steps.consequence: They can see what size is appropriate when they arrive.
steps.quote: Show the suggested size of a swap portion with a real example near the door, saving newcomers the awkwardness of guessing what's fair.

steps.premise: Someone may hesitate to make an imperfect mark in a public sketchbook.
steps.action: Let a gardener put an unfinished pencil study near the front.
steps.consequence: Seeing tentative marks makes it easier for another visitor to try drawing.
steps.quote: Let a gardener contribute an unfinished pencil study near the front. A few searching lines make putting an imperfect mark in a public book feel easier.

steps.premise: A whole garden border can be too much to fit on a page.
steps.action: Offer a small cardboard viewfinder to frame part of the border.
steps.consequence: The visitor can pick a manageable group of stems to draw.
steps.quote: A small cardboard viewfinder helps someone faced with a whole border pick a patch of stems that fits on the page.

steps.premise: Another visitor may want to see the plant shown in a sketch.
steps.action: Leave space by the drawing to record where the plant grows in the garden.
steps.consequence: The reader can find the plant and examine the detail in person.
steps.quote: Leave space for the plant's garden location beside a drawing, helping another visitor track down an intriguing seed head for a closer look.

steps.premise: Some visitors want to test a mark before putting it in a shared book.
steps.action: Put scrap paper in the pencil tray.
steps.consequence: Visitors can try the mark privately before committing it to the book.
steps.quote: Keep a few pieces of scrap paper in the pencil tray for people who want to try a mark privately before committing it to the shared book.

steps.premise: Visitors need a close view to draw small plant details.
steps.action: Invite them to draw the fallen pods already on the table.
steps.consequence: They can examine and draw those details without picking anything.
steps.quote: An invitation to draw the fallen pods already on the table brings small details within reach without asking visitors to pick anything.

steps.premise: Some visitors enjoy observing quietly.
steps.action: Occasionally hold a quiet drawing period before a garden tour.
steps.consequence: They can try the shared sketchbooks alongside others while observing in silence.
steps.quote: Offer an occasional quiet drawing period before a garden tour, letting visitors who like to observe in silence try the books in company.

steps.premise: A performer’s travel delay can leave a usable opening in the fitting schedule.
steps.action: Give performers one named person to notify when delayed.
steps.consequence: The team can reassign the time while the opening is still available.
steps.quote: Let performers send word to one named contact if their journey is delayed, so the team can fill a gap while there's still time to use it.

steps.premise: Finished costumes may get mixed in with garments needing work during cleanup.
steps.action: Reserve a rail for stage-ready garments.
steps.consequence: They stay out of the alterations pile at the end of the evening.
steps.quote: Reserve a rail for garments ready to go onstage, keeping them out of the alterations pile when the room is cleared at the end.

steps.premise: The fitter needs to keep appointments on pace while attending to the performer.
steps.action: Put a legible clock where the fitter can see it.
steps.consequence: The fitter can track time without repeatedly turning away.
steps.quote: Keep an easy-to-read clock within the fitter's sight so they can pace an appointment without repeatedly looking away from the performer.

steps.premise: Owners may limit what the team can change on a borrowed garment.
steps.action: Mark borrowed garments on the rail with the owner’s alteration limits.
steps.consequence: A volunteer can avoid changes the owner has ruled out, such as shortening a protected hem.
steps.quote: Mark borrowed pieces on the rail with the owner's alteration limits, saving a volunteer from shortening a hem that must be returned intact.

steps.premise: Some changes need another fitting and the wearer and garment are available now.
steps.action: Circle those changes and agree on a return time with the wearer at the fitting.
steps.consequence: The team knows which work to recheck and when the wearer will return.
steps.quote: Circle any change that needs another fitting and agree on a return time with the wearer, while their schedule and the garment are both to hand.

steps.premise: The sewing workload may exceed what the team can finish.
steps.action: Record the priorities the team has agreed on.
steps.consequence: Urgent work such as a costume for the next rehearsal can be done in time.
steps.quote: Write down the agreed priorities if there's more sewing than the team can finish, so a costume needed at tomorrow's rehearsal gets attention in time.

steps.premise: A learner may be unsure whether an opponent welcomes questions during a game.
steps.action: Designate a couple of tables where players welcome spoken questions.
steps.consequence: Learners can ask about a move knowing questions are acceptable there.
steps.quote: Keep a couple of tables for games where spoken questions are welcome, so a learner can ask about a move without guessing whether their opponent minds.

steps.premise: Showing a position beside an ongoing match can draw a crowd around the players.
steps.action: Put a demonstration board in a corner away from active matches.
steps.consequence: A helper can show the position without drawing onlookers around someone else’s game.
steps.quote: Place a demonstration board in a corner away from active games, giving a helper room to show a position without gathering a crowd around someone else's match.

steps.premise: The beep ending one game can distract players nearby.
steps.action: Mute the communal chess clocks.
steps.consequence: Neighboring players can keep concentrating when another game ends.
steps.quote: Silence the beeps on communal clocks so the end of one game doesn't break a neighboring player's concentration.

steps.premise: Children practising a move need pieces while games may be in progress.
steps.action: Give those children their own set to practise with.
steps.consequence: They can try moves without taking pieces from a live game.
steps.quote: Give children who want to practise piece movement a set of their own, so they can explore how a knight jumps without borrowing from a live game.

steps.premise: Arriving visitors may want to see how busy the room is.
steps.action: Keep the view from the entrance to the playing tables unobstructed.
steps.consequence: Visitors can assess the room before walking through the playing area.
steps.quote: Keep the sightline from the entrance to the tables open, allowing visitors to see whether the room is busy before walking through the playing area.

steps.premise: A beginner may misjudge how long a game will take before closing.
steps.action: Give players a quiet advance notice of closing time.
steps.consequence: The beginner and their opponent have time to agree where to stop.
steps.quote: Give players a quiet heads-up before closing time so a beginner still learning to judge game length can agree on a stopping point with their opponent.
